title: Radical Candor
author: Kim Scott
note: Package-shaped projection (promote-time stripInternalFields applied). Book is UNPUBLISHED; this is a preview of 2 randomly selected chapters (2 and 6) exactly as they would appear in book-packages/radical-candor.v21.json.

chapters.title: Get, Give, and Encourage Guidance
chapters.hook: Who pays when kind silence keeps the one useful fact out of reach?
chapters.counterintuition: Niceness can become the costly move. If you hide the useful fact to save the moment, the person who needs it loses the chance to change.
chapters.tryThisNow: Ask one person in the next 10 minutes: "What did I do this week that made your task harder?"
chapters.keyTakeaway: Ask for criticism first, give praise and correction as specific facts, and help peers speak directly before comfort turns missing truth into lost time.

breakdown.fastRead:
Who pays if Sheryl Sandberg keeps the hard observation quiet? Sandberg keeps the calm minute for herself, and Kim Scott loses a fact she can use. Sandberg was the manager Scott answered to during their Google years, a story Scott made public in 2017, and that standing trust is why direct guidance can land as help instead of shame.

Ruinous Empathy means care without direct challenge. Put plainly, warmth hides the needed fact. That is the price. Guidance culture means praise and criticism move up, down, and across peers. Start by asking for criticism of your own behavior. Then give specific praise and correction. Then encourage feedback between team members, because the person who sees the problem first may not be the boss.
breakdown.deepRead:
The trap is comfort that looks kind. You skip the hard sentence, no one flinches, and the missing fact moves out of reach. Every hidden fact sends the bill to the person you meant to spare.

Sheryl Sandberg and Kim Scott show the cleaner version. Sandberg managed Scott at Google, and Scott told the story publicly in 2017. Trust already exists. Sandberg can make a hard observation, and Scott can hear it as help. The lesson is not to copy a sharp tone. The relationship is part of the mechanism.

Bob shows the failure. At Juice Software, delayed criticism led toward firing. First, Bob lacked the clear fact. Then the problem grew harder for everyone. Last, the real talk carried too much weight. Late truth no longer sounded like help. It sounded like a verdict.

The feedback order of operations keeps the cost where it belongs. Solicit feedback first, which means ask others to criticize your behavior. A go-to question helps because people with less power can prepare an honest answer. Do not treat the first polite reply as the whole answer.

Then give feedback to individuals. Praise counts. Specific praise tells someone what to repeat; vague approval just says you are pleased. Finally, encourage feedback between team members. Peers often see the issue first, and routing each hard fact through the boss slows the fix.
breakdown.fullRead:
Bob's failure is useful because it does not start with a loud mistake. At Juice Software, the soft pass buys a calm minute. Bob does not get the direct criticism. The person holding the fact feels kind, but Bob has less information than the job requires.

Trace the cost. First comes missing data. Bob keeps acting from the facts he has, while the needed fact sits elsewhere. If he guesses wrong, the miss can look like refusal instead of confusion.

Then comes lost time. Each easy exchange protects the speaker and charges Bob. The problem grows harder for everyone. By the time firing is near, the direct fact has to carry months of delay.

That is why the final talk can feel unfair even when the content is true. The hard fact arrives with the weight of a verdict. A useful warning has become late evidence. Who pays for the quiet?

Sandberg's case keeps the cure honest. Sheryl Sandberg managing Kim Scott at Google, in the account Scott published in 2017, is not proof that famous settings make directness right. It shows that trust changes how a hard observation lands. Without that base, the same hard line can sound like force.

This is where the limits live. Obnoxious Aggression means direct challenge without care; accurate criticism can still damage trust when the care signal is missing. Manipulative Insincerity means neither care nor direct challenge; the person protects image or advantage, and truth goes sideways. Silence is not neutral there.

The order is the guardrail. Solicit feedback before giving it. Ask the same plain question often enough that people can prepare a real answer. If the matter is urgent, do not use the order as an excuse to wait. Say the fact with care now, then ask what you should have done sooner.

After that, give feedback to individuals. Praise is not a soft extra. Specific praise tells someone what to repeat, so it belongs beside correction. Vague praise leaves the useful behavior hidden inside a warm feeling.

Then encourage feedback between team members. Peers often see the work first. If every concern waits for the boss, each fix waits too. The boss loses control over every hard sentence, but the people closest to the issue gain speed.

You can use the move with no title. Ask for criticism of your part before you correct someone else's. Name the fact while it can still help. When two people route an issue through you, ask what fact they should take to each other.

A kind delay is still a delay. The Bob story teaches that comfort has an owner: if you take it, the person who needed the fact pays.

examples.title: Standard Left Open
examples.scenario: Can Sheryl Sandberg name the hard standard before anyone knows how Kim Scott will use it? Yes. In the Google years, Sandberg is the senior manager, and she states the hard observation as guidance, not rank. Scott has not yet proved the result. The scene cuts there, with the fact finally available and the outcome still open.
examples.whatToDo: Ask whether the fact can still help. If it can, state the observation while it can affect the outcome, and keep the care signal plain.
examples.whyItMatters: Ask who would pay for silence. Copying the edge without the relationship risks humiliation, while waiting hides the fact altogether.

examples.title: Minute Already Spent
examples.scenario: Kim Scott is already taking in Sheryl Sandberg's hard observation; the demand is in the past. Sandberg, the manager Scott worked for in their Google years, has spent the awkward minute instead of buying comfort. The pause feels sharp. The move works because the relationship can bear direct guidance, and Scott gets the information while it can still matter.
examples.whatToDo: Ask what price is yours, then spend the awkward minute. Keep the fact tied to help, not rank, and stop when the useful point is clear.
examples.whyItMatters: Ask who gains from the minute. The receiver gets the fact before it goes stale, and the giver pays the cost instead of passing it forward.

examples.title: Ask Comes Due
examples.scenario: At the check-in, the earlier promise comes due: solicit feedback before giving it. The first reply is praise, and the manager running the Order of Operations nearly treats that as permission to give feedback to individuals. The miss is pulled back by another ask for criticism of their own behavior.
examples.whatToDo: Ask, "What did I do that made this harder?" Wait through the first polite answer. If the fact cannot wait, say it now and ask after.
examples.whyItMatters: Treat the order as credibility, not delay. Show you can receive criticism, but never let that rule hide a time-sensitive fact.

examples.title: Bob's Late Bill
examples.scenario: After the path toward firing has formed, Bob's manager at Juice Software can only trace the story backward. The first missed turn was delayed criticism. Bob did not get the clear fact early, so the real conversation became harder for everyone. The ending stays outside this scene; the visible bill is lost time.
examples.whatToDo: Skipping costs time first. Ask, "What fact is Bob still missing?" State that behavior before the only remaining talk is a final one.
examples.whyItMatters: Skipping costs fairness too. Late truth can sound like a verdict, because unclear feedback made the problem grow while everyone felt kind.

examples.title: Outside the Boss Path
examples.scenario: The lead first feels the drag outside the boss path: a peer sees the issue before the boss does. In the Order of Operations, after solicit feedback and give feedback to individuals, every hard fact still waits for one clearinghouse. After peers encourage feedback between team members, the fact reaches the person who can use it.
examples.whatToDo: Ask why this works: peers often see the task first. Have the people closest to the issue carry the fact to each other before it waits upward.
examples.whyItMatters: Ask what control costs: speed. When one boss clears every hard truth, the fix waits; direct peer guidance removes that delay.

examples.title: Praise With a Signal
examples.scenario: Is praise really guidance? Yes, if it tells the person what to repeat. In the Order of Operations, give feedback to individuals can still go wrong before peers encourage feedback between team members. Praise says only that the result was good. The note line stays blank. The miss is pulled back when praise names the observable behavior.
examples.whatToDo: Ask what should be repeated, then praise the observed behavior. Do not save specificity only for criticism; positive guidance needs a visible fact.
examples.whyItMatters: Ask what vague praise hides. It hides the useful move inside approval, so the person feels liked but cannot find the behavior again.

questions.prompt: During a volunteer shift, a coordinator keeps a weak habit comfortable until the helper has no chance to fix it. What caused the failure?
choices: The coordinator saved the hard fact for the most senior volunteer, so the helper heard status before help.
The coordinator made the correction sharp only at the end, so the helper mistook force for care.
The coordinator withheld a useful fact for comfort, so the helper missed the window to change.
questions.explanation: The failure is care without direct challenge. The senior-volunteer answer borrows authority, but the cause is simpler: the useful fact stayed hidden while change was possible.

questions.prompt: When a club chair hears only polite approval, which first move makes honest upward input more likely?
choices: Ask for criticism only after a visible failure, so helpers know the chair wants practical input, not status.
Let an assistant collect concerns first, so rank does not make the chair's request feel heavy.
Use the same plain question often, so helpers can prepare criticism before being put on the spot.
questions.explanation: The repeated question lowers the cost of speaking up. Asking only after a failure uses the right tool at the wrong trigger and makes candor episodic.

questions.prompt: A clinic supervisor admires Sandberg's directness and wants to copy it with a new aide. What should transfer?
choices: Start with the hard edge, so the aide learns high standards before personal comfort enters the talk.
Build enough trust for a hard observation to register as help, not humiliation.
Borrow the senior leader's wording, so the aide hears the correction as proven practice.
questions.explanation: The relationship is part of the mechanism. Borrowed wording is tempting, but it treats the case as style instead of trust carrying a hard point.

questions.prompt: After a lab project stalls, every concern waits for the sponsor though students saw the snag first. What should have happened earlier?
choices: Collect the concerns privately, then have the sponsor choose which student needs correction first, not peers.
Have the students carry the observable fact to each other, because peers often see the issue first.
Ask the sponsor to approve each sentence, so students can be direct without risking mismatch.
questions.explanation: The missed move is peer-to-peer correction. Private collection keeps the sponsor as clearinghouse, which is the delay this sequence removes.

questions.prompt: A startup founder delays a hard conversation because a developer seems fragile. Why is that default costly?
choices: Muddy criticism delays the real talk, so the issue grows harder for the developer and company.
Peer feedback arrives first, so the founder's later correction sounds like an unwanted second opinion from outside the real task.
Specific praise is missing, so the developer cannot tell which strong behavior should be repeated before hearing any concern.
questions.explanation: The Bob case prices delay. Peer input may matter elsewhere, but here the damage is that unclear feedback postpones the direct conversation.

questions.prompt: Before a department head asks staff to be more candid, which action belongs first?
choices: Give each person one clear correction, so the effort begins with standards everyone can see, not soft talk.
Send peers to correct one another, so honesty travels sideways without a boss in the middle.
Invite staff to criticize the head's own behavior, so later correction has proof of receptiveness.
questions.explanation: Get before give proves receptiveness. Starting with downward correction may be clear, but it skips the first proof that criticism can travel upward.

questions.prompt: In a condo vote, a member sees a flaw, stays quiet to avoid looking unprepared, then warns allies after. What damaged trust?
choices: She challenged without care, so the accurate point sounded harsh when the group was deciding.
She guarded her image, so feedback became political while the flaw stayed hidden.
She routed the point through the chair, so the right person heard it too early.
questions.explanation: The damage comes from evasion and side-channel warning. The harshness answer fits direct challenge without care, but this person avoided the direct challenge.

questions.prompt: During a lab handoff, a true criticism leaves the assistant shut down instead of clearer. What explains the miss?
choices: The lead challenged without a care signal, so accuracy damaged trust instead of helping.
The lead asked for criticism first, so the assistant heard the point as shared vulnerability.
The lead praised a repeatable behavior, so the assistant confused approval with correction.
questions.explanation: A true point can fail when care is absent. The upward-feedback answer names a valid step, but the scene shows a hard line that did not carry care.

questions.prompt: Your study partner improves one paragraph, and you want the move repeated later. Which response fits?
choices: Name the paragraph change itself, so your partner knows which behavior to repeat.
Keep praise general, so the warm part stays separate from any later criticism and feels easy to accept.
Ask a stronger writer to validate the praise, so the standard feels established.
questions.explanation: Specific praise is guidance because it marks repeatable behavior. General warmth is tempting, but it hides the very move you want to see again.

reviewCards.front: What comes before you give hard feedback?
reviewCards.back: Ask for criticism of your own behavior. Getting truth first proves that hard information can travel toward you, not only away from you.

reviewCards.front: Why can kind silence become unfair?
reviewCards.back: It can hide the fact a person needs while there is still time to use it. The comfort is yours now, but the lost chance is theirs later.

reviewCards.front: What does Bob at Juice Software warn you to price?
reviewCards.back: Price the delay. Bob, Juice Software, delayed criticism, and firing show how unclear feedback can turn a fixable gap into a late verdict.

reviewCards.front: What should you avoid copying from the Sandberg and Scott case?
reviewCards.back: Do not copy directness as mere style. Sheryl Sandberg managed Kim Scott at Google, and their story, told in 2017, shows that relationship trust helps the hard observation land.

reviewCards.front: What makes praise useful rather than merely warm?
reviewCards.back: Useful praise names the observable behavior to repeat. Vague approval may feel good, but it leaves the repeatable move hidden.

reviewCards.front: Why should peers sometimes speak before the boss path?
reviewCards.back: Peers often see the issue first. Routing every hard fact through one boss slows learning and makes people wait for permission to correct course.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Ask the First Question. Invite criticism of your own behavior before you give a hard line to someone else. Then give praise or correction as a specific fact while it can still help.

ifThenPlans.context: You are about to correct someone and the matter is not urgent.
ifThenPlans.plan: If I have time before I correct, then I will ask: "What did I do that made this harder?"

ifThenPlans.context: You need to give a time-sensitive correction.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the fact cannot wait, then I will say it with care now and ask afterward: "What should I have done sooner?"

ifThenPlans.context: Two peers route the same concern through you.
ifThenPlans.plan: If I become the clearinghouse, then I will ask: "What fact should you take directly to each other?"

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tomorrow noon, draft 1 exact ask you will use before a hard line: "What did I do that made your task harder?"
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Every Friday for 15 minutes, observe where comfort delayed a fact, then note the first ask you will use the following week.

memorableLines.text: Guidance culture means praise and criticism move up, down, and across peers.
Every hidden fact sends the bill to the person you meant to spare.

chapters.title: Guidance
chapters.hook: Direct feedback can help. Everyone agreed; the receiver still paid for careless delivery.
chapters.counterintuition: Directness gets safer when it accepts limits. HHIPP keeps a true message from crossing the wrong line on timing, place, tone, and identity.
chapters.tryThisNow: Cross out one character label in a draft, then say aloud: "When you did X, Y happened; can we look at that?"
chapters.keyTakeaway: Use HHIPP before feedback leaves your mouth: be humble and helpful, act fast, go face to face, keep criticism private, and name behavior rather than character.

breakdown.fastRead:
Direct feedback can help. Everyone agreed; no one knew how to bring back proof without leaving a bruise. The Center for Creative Leadership, the group behind SBI, gives one plain way through it: name the Situation, the Behavior, and the Impact. Small misses travel.

SBI, a Situation, Behavior, Impact method, keeps the line tied to what was seen. HHIPP, the Humble, Helpful, Immediate, In Person, Private, and not Personalized list, guards the delivery. Helpful means useful to the other person, not satisfying to you. Use the list before the sentence leaves your mouth.

The promise holds only on a short clock. Immediate means 2-3 minutes when the context is fresh, not saving the line for later. Private means criticism does not need an audience. Not Personalized means the behavior gets named, not the person's worth.
breakdown.deepRead:
Center for Creative Leadership SBI slows the first impulse just enough to make it usable. You do not start with "you are careless." You start with where it happened, what the person did, and what effect followed. That small route matters because the speaker can be direct without turning the other person into the problem. The sentence travels on facts, not heat.

HHIPP adds the delivery risks SBI does not carry by itself. Humble keeps you open to being partly wrong. Helpful asks whether the line can aid the recipient. Immediate keeps the event close, so memory has not blurred. In Person keeps tone from going thin. Private lowers status threat for criticism. Not Personalized keeps identity out of the charge.

What risk is this member guarding? The answer changes with the miss. A public correction may show standards, but the crowd can turn learning into shame. A late note may sound calm, but the link to the act may be gone. A character label may feel crisp, but it spends trust and buys a fight.

CORE, a Context, Observation, Result, Explore flow from the Radical Candor team (the source group named with CORE), adds one more turn. Explore means the receiver can add facts and help shape what happens after the line lands. That is where a verdict becomes a talk. Directness gets safer when the other side can answer.

The checklist is not a shield for rude speed. It is a ledger. Six risks go out, six balances come back: humility, help, timing, presence, privacy, and behavior. Miss one, and the true part of the message may still fail.
breakdown.fullRead:
A checklist can make directness sound easy, which is exactly where it can fail. If you use HHIPP as a pass to fire off every true thought, the list has become a mask. The six members are not there to make you feel brave. They are there to keep the receiver able to learn.

Center for Creative Leadership SBI shows the first guardrail. Situation answers where and when. Behavior answers what was seen. Impact answers what changed because of it. The method is plain, but it blocks the leap from one act to a whole person. You can say, "In the handoff, the client file moved late, and the queue stalled," without saying, "You are lazy." One line can cross a lot of ground.

HHIPP then asks whether the line should move now, where it should land, and what it should leave untouched. Immediate does not mean blurting in the hallway. It means 2-3 minutes while the facts still sit near the act. In Person does not mean dragging someone into a show. It means tone and care can be read. Private means criticism is not made heavier by status loss.

Praise can be public because the status effect helps. Criticism is different. The audience changes the lesson into a display, and the recipient must now manage both the content and the social hit. If the aim is learning, privacy is not softness. It is the route that lets the useful part arrive.

Not Personalized is the member many people skip when they feel sure. Character words are fast. Careless, lazy, defensive, and sloppy all give the speaker a clean villain. They also trap the other person inside a trait. Behavior words keep change possible. What was done? What happened because of it? What can move now?

CORE brings the line back to dialogue. Context, Observation, and Result are close kin to SBI, but Explore matters because the speaker may not have the whole ledger. The receiver may know a fact the speaker missed. The receiver may accept the effect but see a better repair. Without Explore, the promise comes back as a verdict, and verdicts make people defend before they think.

The go-to question works on the same rule from the other side. A repeated prompt for direct reports makes upward criticism less vague. If you ask, "Any feedback?" the door is wide and easy to dodge. If you ask the same concrete question often, people know which path to take. The proof comes after you are criticized, not before.

Rewarding criticism closes the loop. A private thank-you may be kind, but people watch for visible proof that candor mattered. What changed after the hard line was said? If nothing moves, the ledger does not balance. The next honest person may decide silence is cheaper.

This can help even without title power. You can use SBI on your own promises, peer notes, and handoffs. You can cross out a character word before you send a message. You can ask for one clear critique and then show what changed. Guidance is not rank. Guidance is care made specific enough to be used.

Use the opposite move when safety, law, or urgent command needs a clear order. Do not Explore while a risk is still live and seconds matter. Do not make a private criticism public to prove nerve. Do not soften a fact until it vanishes. The list helps when the person can learn from the line; it fails when you use it to dodge a needed call or to dress up a blow.

examples.title: HHIPP Skipped at the Standard
examples.scenario: A team lead has a true criticism ready and the standard in hand: HHIPP names six members, including not Personalized, and directness alone does not qualify. She skips the list. The criticism lands in the open room, days late, aimed at character. The receiver hears a status hit before hearing the behavior that could change.
examples.whatToDo: Read the cost before you speak: move the criticism private, make it quick enough to link to the act, and cross out the character label.
examples.whyItMatters: Skipping HHIPP spends more than it saves. Truth without delivery care can buy shame, delay, and defense instead of change.

examples.title: SBI Pulls Back the Impression
examples.scenario: Center for Creative Leadership SBI is already in use when the line starts to drift. The speaker has said the effect, but the middle is still a general impression. The miss is close: "careless" would settle the matter too broadly. Situation and Behavior pull the sentence back before Impact turns into blame.
examples.whatToDo: The sentence works because SBI forces the speaker to pass through where, what, and effect before the judgment can harden.
examples.whyItMatters: The method pays off by making the feedback verifiable. A general impression can be denied; a seen act can be changed.

examples.title: CORE Leaves the Door Open
examples.scenario: What keeps a verdict from staying a verdict? On the call, the Radical Candor team's CORE reaches the return point at Explore. Context, Observation, and Result have been named, and the earlier commitment is now answered by the receiver's turn. The speaker does not yet know what facts will come back or whether the repair will hold.
examples.whatToDo: The question opens the answer: after Context, Observation, and Result, ask the receiver what else needs to be known.
examples.whyItMatters: The turn keeps feedback from becoming a one-way sentence. Explore lets missing facts enter before the repair moves.

examples.title: SBI Pays the Cost
examples.scenario: Center for Creative Leadership SBI has already done its job, and the folded page shows the cost. The speaker gave up the quick label, named the situation, named the behavior, and kept impact tied to what changed. The line took longer. The receiver got something usable.
examples.whatToDo: The page says: pay the cost of detail before you name the effect.
examples.whyItMatters: The trade is clear: less speed, more change.

examples.title: The Direct Report Sees Proof
examples.scenario: HHIPP first reaches the direct report on the call after the go-to question has been asked; the 2-3 minutes after criticism will decide whether the answer counts. Private thanks alone is heading for a miss. Visible reward pulls it back: the criticized behavior changes, so future candor has proof.
examples.whatToDo: The proof must be visible: ask the same clear prompt, thank the person, and show one change that came from the criticism.
examples.whyItMatters: The witness is downstream. Reward criticism where people can see it, or the next true line may never leave the sender.

questions.prompt: A trainer turns HHIPP into a broad culture slogan for every trust issue. What is actually wrong with that use?
choices: The trainer is applying HHIPP too late, after feedback has already lost its context.
The trainer is using a delivery checklist as if it were a general culture label.
The trainer is skipping Private, because turning the list into a slogan makes every criticism public.
questions.explanation: HHIPP belongs to feedback mechanics, not every culture problem. It is a delivery checklist, so treating it as a wide slogan stretches the tool beyond its job.

questions.prompt: During a standup, a lead wants to correct one person so the standard is clear. Which choice fits HHIPP?
choices: Save both praise and criticism for a later private conversation so no peer can compare status.
Correct the person in front of peers, then soften the status hit with a helpful tone.
Move criticism private, while allowing praise to stay public when it helps the person.
questions.explanation: Private guards against turning criticism into shame. The public-standard choice is tempting, but the audience adds status threat and can block learning.

questions.prompt: Your draft is true and direct, but it ignores delivery risks. Which revision uses the full HHIPP guardrail?
choices: Keep the message direct if the facts are sound, then fix tone only if the receiver objects.
Make the line humble and helpful, but leave timing and privacy for later judgment.
Make it humble, helpful, quick, face to face, private for criticism, and aimed at behavior.
questions.explanation: The full list matters because each member guards a different risk. A true line can still fail if timing, privacy, or identity language is skipped.

questions.prompt: A peer says, "You seemed off all morning," and cannot name what happened. What is the best next move?
choices: State where it happened, what was observed, and what changed so the claim can be checked.
Ask whether the peer has enough proof to make the same impression public and hard to dispute.
Delay the comment until a formal review gives the impression more weight.
questions.explanation: SBI forces observable specificity. The proof choice still leaves a general impression in charge; the useful move is to name where, what, and effect.

questions.prompt: When your direct reports keep dodging upward criticism, which request lowers the ambiguity?
choices: Ask for any thoughts whenever people seem ready, so the request keeps a broad scope.
Use the same go-to question so people know exactly how to criticize upward.
Wait for stronger evidence that people want to speak before asking again.
questions.explanation: A repeated prompt gives people a clear path. A vague open request sounds kind, but it is easy to dodge because no one knows what kind of critique is wanted.

questions.prompt: A note says, "You are lazy with handoffs," though the missed act is clear. Which principle does it break?
choices: It uses the right behavior focus but sends the message after context has faded.
It attacks character instead of naming behavior and impact that can change.
It makes the criticism private when praise would have been better in public.
questions.explanation: Not Personalized keeps the person out of the charge. The timing answer is a near miss only if delay is the issue; here the identity label is the break.

questions.prompt: After a direct report criticizes your choice, you thank them in private and change nothing. What happens downstream?
choices: Future honesty gets less safe because people see no proof that candor mattered.
The private thanks is enough because reward works best when no one else sees it.
The criticism should wait for a later review so the reaction can feel less tense.
questions.explanation: People watch the reaction to criticism. Private thanks may sound respectful, but without visible reward or change, the ledger teaches silence.

questions.prompt: In a feedback talk, Context, Observation, and Result are clear. Which move keeps it from becoming a one-way verdict?
choices: Add Explore so the receiver can add facts and help shape what comes after.
Stop after Result, since extra discussion may weaken the feedback and blur the point.
Move back to Situation and Behavior to make the first claim more exact.
questions.explanation: Explore invites dialogue after the observed result is named. Repeating earlier parts may add detail, but it still can leave the receiver outside the repair.

questions.prompt: A supervisor stores every criticism for a scheduled review so the wording can be cleaner. What is the likely cost?
choices: The feedback may become too private for the recipient to connect it with behavior.
The criticism may sound too humble, so the standard will be hard to hear.
The context can fade, making the person less able to link the line to the act.
questions.explanation: Immediate means close to the behavior, often within 2-3 minutes. Waiting for a later review can make the act harder to recall and use.

reviewCards.front: What are the six HHIPP members, and why do they belong together?
reviewCards.back: HHIPP means Humble, Helpful, Immediate, In Person, Private, and not Personalized. They belong together because directness needs delivery limits, not just true content.

reviewCards.front: How does SBI stop feedback from becoming a vague impression?
reviewCards.back: SBI makes the speaker name the Situation, the Behavior, and the Impact. That keeps the line tied to what was observed instead of a mood about the person.

reviewCards.front: What does not Personalized require you to remove from criticism?
reviewCards.back: Remove character labels. Name the act and its effect instead, because identity attacks make defense more likely while behavior language leaves room for change.

reviewCards.front: Why does CORE add Explore after Context, Observation, and Result?
reviewCards.back: Explore gives the receiver a turn. They can add missing facts and help shape what happens after the feedback, so the line does not stay a one-way verdict.

reviewCards.front: Why does a repeated go-to question work better than a vague request for feedback?
reviewCards.back: The repeated prompt lowers ambiguity. People know what kind of upward criticism is wanted, while a broad request is easy to dodge without seeming unhelpful.

reviewCards.front: What proof do people need after they criticize upward?
reviewCards.back: They need visible reward that candor mattered. Thanks helps, but future honesty gets safer when people can see a real response or change.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Cross-Out Careless Feedback. Before you say or send criticism, remove one word that judges the person and replace it with the observed behavior and effect. Then check timing and privacy so the line can be heard.

ifThenPlans.context: If your draft uses a character word like lazy, careless, or defensive
ifThenPlans.plan: If the draft names a trait, then cross out that word and write the situation, behavior, and impact instead.

ifThenPlans.context: If the behavior just happened and the facts are still fresh
ifThenPlans.plan: If the moment is still clear, then give the line in 2-3 minutes rather than storing it for later.

ifThenPlans.context: If criticism would land in front of an audience
ifThenPlans.plan: If people are watching, then move the criticism private and keep any public comment for praise.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Spend 5 minutes today: cross out one character label and pre-write one exact sentence to say or send, using behavior plus impact.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Audit three feedback drafts for timing, privacy, and character labels before they leave.

memorableLines.text: Use the list before the sentence leaves your mouth.
The proof comes after you are criticized, not before.
Helpful means useful to the other person, not satisfying to you.
